I'm mapping out the grid coordinates row by row, tracing which cells are filled to identify the distinct shapes across the 11x11 layout.

Tracing connectivity, I find one large blob of 15 connected cells forming an irregular shape in the upper-left area, then a separate 5-cell piece near the bottom-left resembling a T with a tail, and a 4-cell T-tetromino in the middle. I'm now checking the right side of the grid starting around r1c7-c9 to identify the remaining shapes.

Following the right-side cells further, I trace out a 10-cell connected region and a separate 9-cell region below it. Now I have six candidate shapes with sizes 15, 5, 4, 4, 10, 9, and I'm testing whether the T-tetromino could evenly divide into the 10-cell or 15-cell shapes—neither works since 10 and 15 aren't multiples of 4.

Now I'm checking whether a size-5 shape could compose the 10-cell or 15-cell shapes, since 10/5=2 and 15/5=3 could work, so I'm normalizing coordinates for both shapes to compare them directly.

Testing the 10-shape, I find placing one copy of the T-with-stem prototype in the top rows leaves exactly a rotated mirror copy of the same shape behind, confirming the 10-shape decomposes into two prototype copies, while the 9-shape gets ruled out since 9 isn't divisible by 5. Now I'm moving to check whether the 15-shape splits into three copies as well.

I extract one prototype-shaped piece (a bar of three cells with a two-cell stem centered above) from the top of the 15-shape, then start hunting for the next matching piece among the remaining cells.

For the leftover cells, a vertical bar of three with a horizontal stem of two extending from its center fits nicely, giving me piece2. Then the final leftover cells — a bar in row4 with a stem going down at the center — match the prototype too, confirming that 15 pieces decompose cleanly.

Since size 5 isn't a multiple of 4, it can't be built from smaller pieces itself, but it does combine to form both the 10-shape and 15-shape, making it the true prototype. The 9-shape and the tetrominoes don't compose or get composed by anything else, so they get dropped, leaving the kept shapes as the 5-shape, 10-shape, and 15-shape built from it.

Now I'm working out row by row which cells survive after removing the disqualified shapes, mapping out exactly which columns remain in each row from r0 through r10.

I'm placing shape F across cols 6-8 in that row, then considering whether a 3x3 square or S-tetromino could work in the remaining space—but I realize the 3x3 can't be tiled by L-trominoes and the tetromino doesn't divide evenly into the other shapes, so I'm ruling those out.

Let me try a second example with domino as the prototype instead: checking which shapes like the 2x2 square and L-tetromino can be built from dominoes, while single cells and the plus-pentomino get removed since they aren't composable.
